'''''Rosa rubiginosa''''' ('''sweet briar''',<ref name=rhs/> '''sweetbriar rose''',<ref>{{PLANTS|id=RORU82|taxon=Rosa rubiginosa |access-date=23 October 2015}}</ref> '''sweet brier''' or '''eglantine''';<ref name=rhs>{{cite web |url=http://www.rhs.org.uk/plants/details?plantid=1705 |title=''Rosa rubiginosa'' |publisher=The Royal Horticultural Society |access-date=26 July 2014}}</ref> [[synonym (taxonomy)|syn.]] ''R. eglanteria'') is a species of [[rose]] native to [[Europe]] and western [[Asia]].

==Description==
[[Image:Rosa rubiginosa sl20.jpg|upright|thumb|left|''Rosa rubiginosa'' sepals, prickles, glandular hairs]]
[[Image:20140110Rosa rubiginosa1.jpg|thumb|left|171px|Ripe fruits (called "hips")]]
It is a dense [[deciduous]] [[shrub]] {{Convert|2-3|m|ft|sp=us}} high and across, with the stems bearing numerously hooked [[Spine (botany)|prickles]]. The [[foliage]] has a strong [[apple]]-like fragrance. The [[leaf|leaves]] are pinnately compound, {{Convert abbreviated|5-9|cm}} long, with 5–9 rounded to oval leaflets with a serrated margin, and numerous glandular hairs. The [[flower]]s are 1.8–3 cm in diameter, the five petals being pink with a white base, and the numerous stamens yellow; the flowers are produced in clusters of 2–7 together, from late spring to mid-summer. The fruit is a globose to oblong red [[rose hip|hip]] 1–2 cm in diameter.

==Etymology==
Its name ''eglantine'' is from [[Middle English]] {{Lang|enm|eglentyn}}, from [[Old French]] {{Lang|fro|aiglantin}} (adj.), from ''aiglent'' 'sweetbrier', from [[Vulgar Latin]] *''aculentus'' (with the ending of ''spinulentus'' 'thorny, prickly'), from Latin {{Lang|la|aculeus}} 'prickle', from {{Lang|la|acus}} 'needle'. ''Sweet'' refers to the sweet, apple fragrance of the leaves, while ''briar'' ~ ''brier'' refers to it being a thorny bush.<ref>Vedel, H. & Lange, J. (1960). ''Trees and bushes''. Metheun, London.</ref>

==Distribution and habitat==
''Rosa rubiginosa'' is native to most of Europe with the exception of the extreme north (above [[61st parallel north|61°N]]), where it inhabits pastures and thorny bushes from the [[Montane ecosystems|montane]] to the [[subalpine]] floor, with a sunny, continental climate. It is somewhat rare, with isolated specimens near roads and pastures frequented by cattle. Its presence is doubtful in western Asia. In [[Southern Europe]] it lives in higher altitudes, usually {{cvt|1000|to|1700|m}}.<ref>{{cite web |title=''Rosa rubiginosa'' |url=http://www.floraiberica.es/floraiberica/texto/pdfs/06_087_13%20Rosa.pdf |publisher=[[Flora Iberica]] |access-date=11 April 2021}}</ref> In [[Portugal]] it is classified as [[Critically Endangered]] and is restricted to the [[Serra da Estrela]] range.<ref>{{cite web |title=''Rosa rubiginosa'' L. |url=https://flora-on.pt/#/1Rosa+rubiginosa |publisher=[[Flora-On]] |access-date=11 April 2021}}</ref>

==Cultivation and uses==
In addition to its pink flowers, it is valued for its scent and the hips that form after the flowers and persist well into the winter.{{cn|date=July 2025}}

During [[World War II]], the British relied on rose hips and [[hops]] as presumed sources of [[vitamin A|vitamins A]] and [[vitamin C|C]], leading to the British wartime expression: "We are getting by on our hips and hops."<ref name="proverb">{{Cite web |date=2016-11-04 |title=Herbs - Quotes and Proverbs |url=https://quoteproverbs.com/herbs/ |access-date=2021-11-15 |website=QuoteProverbs |language=en-US}}</ref>

==Invasive species==
''Rosa rubiginosa'' has become an [[invasive species]] in most of [[Patagonia|Argentine Patagonia]] and in the south of [[Chile]], particularly where the steppe meets the forest. Cattle spread the seed efficiently through their feces. Poor knowledge of how detrimental it is to the local economy and native species has led ''Rosa rubiginosa'' to become an existing invasive threat, causing several millions of dollars' worth of damage each year.<ref>{{cite web | url=https://www.rionegro.com.ar/rosa-mosqueta-una-especie-que-atenta-contra-la-ganaderia-CY6032444/ | title=Rosa mosqueta: Una especie que atenta contra la ganadería | date=22 November 2018 }}</ref> It is an invasive species in southeast [[Australia]],<ref>[http://www.weeds.org.au/cgi-bin/weedident.cgi?tpl=plant.tpl&ibra=all&card=S24 Sweet Briar] {{webarchive |url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070928011330/http://www.weeds.org.au/cgi-bin/weedident.cgi?tpl=plant.tpl&ibra=all&card=S24 |date=2007-09-28 }}, weeds.org.au, Accessed 2007-01-24</ref> and is classified as a restricted plant in New Zealand banned from sale, propagation and distribution in the Auckland,<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.arc.govt.nz/albany/index.cfm?63E0F20E-14C2-3D2D-B905-50098EBBE4B9&plantcode=Rosrub |title=Plant details - sweet briar |publisher=ARC |access-date=11 February 2011 |archive-date=7 February 2013 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130207101506/http://www.arc.govt.nz/albany/index.cfm?63E0F20E-14C2-3D2D-B905-50098EBBE4B9&plantcode=Rosrub }}</ref> Canterbury,<ref>{{cite web |url=http://ecan.govt.nz/advice/your-land/plant-animal-pests/Pages/rules-plant-pests.aspx |title=Rules for plant pests |publisher=Ecan |access-date=11 February 2011 |archive-date=13 September 2016 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160913210145/http://ecan.govt.nz/advice/your-land/plant-animal-pests/Pages/rules-plant-pests.aspx }}</ref> and Southland regions. The [[New Zealand Department of Conservation]] classifies ''R. rubiginosa'' as an "environmental weed".<ref>{{cite book |last=Howell |first=Clayson |title=Consolidated list of environmental weeds in New Zealand |publisher=Department of Conservation |location=Wellington |date=May 2008 |series=DRDS292 |url=http://www.doc.govt.nz/upload/documents/science-and-technical/drds292.pdf |isbn=978-0-478-14413-0 |access-date=2009-05-06}}</ref> The plant is present in extensive areas of pasture and [[tussock grassland]]s in the [[Otago]] and [[Canterbury, New Zealand|Canterbury]] regions, where the seeds are spread by cattle, [[common brushtail possum|possum]]s and birds that eat the hips. Growth from seed is aided by the reduction in competing pasture by rabbits.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.massey.ac.nz/massey/learning/colleges/college-of-sciences/clinics-and-services/weeds-database/sweet-brier.cfm |title=Sweet brier |website=Weeds Database |date=16 August 2016 |publisher=Massey University |access-date=22 January 2017}}</ref> It is listed as a Category 1 Declared Weed in [[South Africa]]. These plants may no longer be planted or propagated, and all trade in their seeds, cuttings or other propagative material is prohibited.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.plantzafrica.com/miscell/aliens1.htm |title=Declared Weeds & Alien Invader Plants |publisher=South African National Biodiversity Institute |access-date=13 June 2014 |archive-date=4 March 2016 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160304055157/http://www.plantzafrica.com/miscell/aliens1.htm }}</ref>
